title: ‘We believe she’s still there’: Family searches for Bartlett woman missing in devastating Nepal flood - Chicago Tribune
description: ‘We believe she’s still there’: Family searches for Bartlett woman missing in devastating Nepal flood  Chicago Tribune
publisher.title: Chicago Tribune
full_article:
Family members of a Bartlett woman who went missing in last week’s massive flood in Nepal have been in Kathmandu since Monday hoping to find her and bring her home safe.

Poonam Thakkar, 42, embarked Aug. 20 on a holy pilgrimage to Mount Kailash near Nepal’s border with Tibet. She was following in the footsteps of her oldest sister, Bhumika, who made the journey a year ago.

Now Bhumika and two cousins have traveled to Nepal to retrace the path Poonam was on when she vanished during the Aug. 26 flood, middle sister Gunjan said Wednesday.

“They intend to visit that impacted area because we believe she’s still there,” Gunjan said.

Their hope is strong, she added, because people have been found alive throughout the week since the flood — blamed on the collapse of a glacier in the Himalayas — despite the official death toll exceeding 1,100 as of Wednesday. Nearly 4,000 others remain missing.

(Manan Vatsyayana/Getty-AFP) Expand

Poonam left Chicago on Aug. 20 for an organized tour to the Tibet border that was to begin Aug. 23. Family members last spoke to her by phone the day before the flood.

“It was all casual, and she was just sharing how excited she was to be starting the pilgrimage,” Gunjan said. “She was enjoying every minute of it.”

Poonam has dual citizenship in the U.S. and Canada, having worked in Canada before joining her sisters and immediate family in Bartlett 7½ years ago, Gunjan said. Extended family also lives in Chicago.

Poonam is a senior manager for one of the big four consulting firms and colleagues have reached out to the family with support, Gunjan said.

Bhumika had wanted to leave for Nepal the day after the flood, but authorities weren’t encouraging travelers that quickly. By the time the three family members left, securing a flight to Nepal was relatively easy.

For now, they are unable to travel beyond Kathmandu, but the family has been in touch with authorities — including from the U.S. and Canadian embassies — whose answers have been compassionate but standard, Gunjan said.

They’ve also met with others seeking loved ones who are missing. They have formed groups that meet each morning to divide up their shared tasks for the day and then collaborate over their findings, according to Gunjan.

While the part of the country they’re hoping to reach continues to be plagued by rain, mudslides and power issues, Kathmandu has been a relatively safe base to operate from, Gunjan said.

While the search for information — and Poonam herself — goes on, Gunjan asks those reading about her sister to hold positive thoughts and wishes for her safe return.

title: Nepal devastation felt in Hudson Valley, as local communities step in to help - News12 | Hudson Valley
description: Nepal devastation felt in Hudson Valley, as local communities step in to help  News12 | Hudson Valley
publisher.title: News12 | Hudson Valley
full_article:
T he devastation in Nepal is being felt in the Hudson Valley, despite the two locations being thousands of miles apart.

At the restaurant Himalaya Yorktown, Nordhen Lama and his father stay busy.

"We've been operating this restaurant for over a decade," said Lama.

But their hearts are also with another part of the world.

"My family, my friends and I were in utter shock. We see the flash floods being surfaced online, sweeping away villages, sweeping away homes and these are actual people living in these homes," Lama told News 12.

Lama's parents are from Nepal and he still has family there.

"My immediate family members are thankfully OK. However, the people in my community, their families have been impacted by this event, and so our hearts mourn for them," said Lama.

That devastation is being felt in other parts of the Hudson Valley too.

Assemblymember Sarahana Shrestha says she's proud to be the first New York state legislator of Nepali origin.

"I spent my first 20 or 21 years of my life in Nepal, and I still have a lot of family there," said Shrestha.

She says her family is OK.

"The real concern is the magnitude of this event. Now people are really on the lookout and are alert for subsequent disasters that could come out of this, whether it's flooding or whether it's recurring climate incidents," Shrestha explained.

Back in Yorktown, Lama says his community is doing what they can to help.

"I know that we, as a nation of Nepal, are very resilient and we will find a way to deal with this for sure," said Lama.

title: More than one week on from Nepal's floods, thousands of children remain without safe water and face rising risk of disease - UNICEF
description: More than one week on from Nepal's floods, thousands of children remain without safe water and face rising risk of disease  UNICEF
publisher.title: UNICEF
full_article:
KATHMANDU, 3 September 2026 – More than one week after flash floods swept down the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river basin in Nepal, at least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene support, UNICEF said today.

Water supply systems have been damaged across the affected districts, from community schemes to larger networks, while sanitation facilities have been damaged and destroyed. At the same time, families are crowded into host households and holding centres, creating conditions that raise the risk of waterborne and infectious disease outbreaks.

“Every parent in these districts is now making the same calculation several times a day,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative in Nepal. “Where can I get water, and is it safe to give to my child? When water systems and toilets have been damaged or destroyed, and dozens of people are sharing the same space, families face enormous challenges in maintaining safe hygiene. The risk of waterborne disease increases rapidly in these conditions, but it is preventable. That is why ensuring access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene is among our top priorities right now.”

UNICEF has dispatched critical water, sanitation, and hygiene supplies for around 19,000 people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. These include more than 3,800 hygiene kits, 3,300 collapsible 10-litre jerrycans, 3,500 buckets, 3,500 one-litre mugs, 4,000 bottles of water treatment solution, and more than 1,000 tarpaulin sheets.

UNICEF is working with government counterparts and partners on disease surveillance, hygiene promotion, and outbreak prevention, with messages on safe hygiene, water handling, and household water treatment being carried through mobile messaging, radio, social media, and community networks. Mobile subscribers can reach validated advisories without data charges, and a network of more than 600 practitioners is extending outreach into affected communities.

As access improves, UNICEF will scale up emergency water supply, household water treatment and water-quality monitoring, temporary sanitation and handwashing facilities, and essential hygiene and menstrual hygiene supplies in communities and holding centres.

“Restoring communities’ access to safe water and sanitation is not a one-week job,” said Akunga. “We can provide water treatment products and emergency supplies today, and we are. But damaged water systems, pipelines, pumps, toilets and other sanitation infrastructure also need to be repaired and rebuilt. And they need to be rebuilt to withstand future floods, not simply restored to the way they were before. We need to make communities safer and more resilient. Otherwise, we will be having the same conversation again after the next disaster, and it will be children paying the price yet again.”

title: Church in Nepal Helps Flood Victims Find Hope, Apostolic Administrator Says - National Catholic Register
description: Church in Nepal Helps Flood Victims Find Hope, Apostolic Administrator Says  National Catholic Register
publisher.title: National Catholic Register
full_article:
Father Silas Bogati, apostolic administrator of the apostolic vicariate of Nepal, said the Catholic Church, a small minority of about 10,000 faithful in the Asian nation, is committed to aiding those affected by the recent major flooding.

According to authorities, the number of dead from last week’s flood exceeds 1,000, while more than 4,000 people remain missing across both countries, CNN reported.

“By being there, providing relief now and, later, contributing to reconstruction, we give hope. Our presence among those who are suffering will give them hope,” the priest said in an interview with the pontifical foundation Aid to the Church in Need (ACN).

Father Bogati explained that in Nepal, “the Catholic Church has 13 parishes and 10,000 Catholics, but it has always worked for the Nepali population irrespective of their religion, and we will continue to do so as they suffer in this hour of need.”

Caritas Nepal has set up community kitchens and dispatched food supplies for 300 affected families to last for 15 days. Given the forecast of additional rainfall and the fact that many people are still sleeping outdoors, the organization said there is a need for tarpaulins, blankets, and sleeping mats.

After noting that “no Catholic churches or chapels have been destroyed,” the Nepalese priest recalled that “the Holy Father, Pope Leo, was the first to pray and to show his sympathy and closeness to the victims of these flash floods. In the same way, we are receiving prayers and support from the Catholic Church around the world.”

Leo XIV has encouraged prayers for those affected and for rescue teams, and has urged the international community to provide aid in a spirit of solidarity.

Father Bogati described the affected area of Rasuwa, located on Nepalʼs border with Tibet. He said an important trade route with Tibet runs through the region, as well as the city of Syabrubesi, “one of the main departure points for tourists traveling toward the Langtang Valley.”

One of this concerns is that “members of one of the Catholic communities [who] go down to Syabrubesi to work … may have been swept away by the waters. We do not have any figures yet.”

“All these hotels and settlements were swept away. There has been a high death toll in this area, and the river continued downstream, wreaking havoc across five districts. The flood has caused enormous devastation, as a huge mass of water surged downstream, destroying everything in its path. Some communities are still cut off, and search and rescue operations are proving difficult,” he recounted.

The apostolic administrator asked for prayers for all the victims and those affected by the tragedy, and expressed gratitude for ACN’s closeness and solidarity.

title: Trump Admin Cut Funds For Flood Prediction Tool In Nepal Before Recent Disaster - Yahoo News Singapore
description: Trump Admin Cut Funds For Flood Prediction Tool In Nepal Before Recent Disaster  Yahoo News Singapore
publisher.title: Yahoo News Singapore
full_article:
Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

The Trump Administration last year stopped funding a vital flood prediction program in Nepal as part of massive federal grant cuts proposed by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency. Nearly a year and a half later, more than 1,000 people were killed by flooding in the south Asia country.

Among the foreign aid funds that Congress approved to slash was the SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya program, a collaboration between NASA and the U.S. Agency for International Development.

The tool aimed to "address critical challenges in climate change, food security, water and related disasters, land use, and air quality," according to its website, which states the program concluded in January 2025. However, its unclear whether the DOGE cuts directly led to the program's suspension.

title: Why Nepal floods should worry India - Yahoo
description: Why Nepal floods should worry India  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.

India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.

Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.

And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.

Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.

How many Nepal rivers flow into India?

Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges [Universal Images Group via Getty Images]

Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.

Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_4bea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_4bea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.

Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).

India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.

Which Indian states are most exposed?

Bihar is India's worst flood-prone state [AFP via Getty Images]

Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_4iea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_4iea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.

But the risk extends beyond Bihar.

Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.

Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.

"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.

Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.

When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?

A view of a flood-affected district in India's Bihar in 2008 [AFP via Getty Images]

Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_4sea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_4sea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.

Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.

Second, the river.

Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.

Third, when the water meets India.

How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_53ea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_53ea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.

The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.

So how much depends on Nepal v India?

"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.

How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk

The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_5aea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_5aea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.

According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.

"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.

The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.

How much warning can India get from Nepal?

For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_5hea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_5hea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.

Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.

A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.

India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_5mea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_5mea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.

They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.

And then there's, crucially, the last mile.

A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.

For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".

What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?

The confluence of Dhauliganga and Rishiganga rivers in India's Chamoli district [AFP via Getty Images]

A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.

Advertisement Advertisement #_R_5vea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: none; } @media screen and (max-width: 767.95px) { #_R_5vea6m6l1dinpfiuqq5bH1_ { display: flex; } iframe { max-width: 100vw; } }

Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.

The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.

But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.

Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.

"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.

Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.

"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.

Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.

The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.

So what should worry India the most?

A massive cloudburst triggered heavy rains and flash floods in Dharali, India, in 2025 [Anadolu via Getty Images]

"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.

In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.

Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".

"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.

A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.

That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.

It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.

And then there's climate change.

Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.

High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.

And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.

They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

title: ‘Pitiful’: experts condemn initial US aid contribution for Nepal flood victims - The Guardian
description: ‘Pitiful’: experts condemn initial US aid contribution for Nepal flood victims  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
Aid experts have denounced the US’s “embarrassing” and “pitiful” initial response to the Nepal flood disaster after the US state department announced it was releasing $500,000 in emergency funds to help the relief effort.

The modest sum – which has since been increased – allocated in response to the devastation caused by mudslides in the mountainous Asian country was mocked on social media, where users contrasted it with the amount spent on other Trump administration priorities.

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more

The death toll from last week’s flash floods has passed 1,000, with 4,400 people still unaccounted, according to officials in Nepal and China. Rescue teams are trying to find workers trapped in hydropower tunnels, which were buried in mud.

The US contribution has been upped to $3.6m, which state department officials say will be used to deliver food assistance to feed 10,000 affected households for up to three months, and pay for emergency items such as blankets, mosquito nets and shelter sheets.

However, seasoned humanitarian aid specialists suggest even that contribution is inadequate and say the US response has shrunk to a shadow of its previous capacity by the dismantling of USAID, the country’s main foreign assistance organization, after Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year.

The organization’s functions were taken over by the state department after USAID was terminated as an independent agency in July 2025 after being dismantled by the unofficial “department of government efficiency”, spearheaded by Elon Musk.

The state department says the US continues to support Nepal’s flood early warning system through grants.

However, foreign aid specialists highlighted the initial $500,000 sum as symbolic of the inadequacy of current US efforts compared with what would have been offered before USAID was dissolved. The state department has countered by saying it was “was designed to get immediate assistance moving while assessments were under way” and insisted the dismantling of USAID had “not slowed the US response”.

Mark Ward, a former head of USAID’s disaster response team, who was nicknamed “Mr Disaster” by President George HW Bush because of his prominent role in relief efforts, called the announcement “embarrassing for the United States and a bit of a slap at Nepal”.

Under USAID, Ward said, the amount would have been decided by a disaster assistance response team, which would have been on the ground immediately to assess needs because of the close working relationship the agency had with Nepal, a known natural disaster zone.

“They would have done an assessment very quickly with the Nepalese authorities, and then we would have decided on a number,” said Ward. “I’m sure it would have been a lot more than the figure that we’ve seen.”

His sentiments were echoed by George Ingram, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former staff member of the House of Representatives foreign affairs committee.

“I was embarrassed for America,” he said. “It would have been better for them not to announce it.

“It’s too early to know what the total magnitude of the US assistance should be, but an initial offering of half a million dollars is pitiful. I do not recall a major disaster like this in which the US initial reaction was such a paltry amount.

“They should have said nothing focused on saying we need to figure out what the needs are.”

After news of floods broke last week, Karoline Leavitt, the outgoing White House press secretary, said the US embassy in Nepal was “in close contact with local authorities on the ground”.

“We’ve offered our help and assistance but of course, the first priority for this president and for Secretary Rubio will always be Americans,” she told Fox News. “We’re focused on rescuing every American that we possibly can.”

Ward, who worked on previous disasters in Nepal, said it was the country that the USAID had the closest relationship with because of its susceptibility to earthquakes and other natural catastrophes with humanitarian consequences.

“There was no country that we had a better relationship with than Nepal in their disaster management capacity, for the simple reason that nobody has more disasters than Nepal because of its topography,” he said. “We always had disaster experts there on our staff working with these guys, getting them ready for the next disaster, and they’re obviously gone now, with the dismantling of USAID.”

Current relief efforts are now being led by Nepal’s neighbors, India and China, said Ward, who argued that the US decision to skimp on foreign aid was a false economy.

“Is it really in the interest of the United States to have China and India in the lead?” he said. “The United States is safer when the world is more stable.

“If the world is unstable, there are more refugees trying to cross borders, and eventually, maybe ours. Maybe American troops have to deploy. So dealing with natural and man-made disasters before they get out of hand is in the interests of the United States, and it’s dirt cheap compared to the kinds of money you need to respond to a civil war, an insurrection or a refugee crisis.”

A state department spokesperson defended the US response as “fast, flexible, and driven by conditions on the ground – not arbitrary funding targets”.

“This is a needs-based, adaptive model that allows the United States to get assistance out the door immediately rather than delay action while waiting for a complete picture of a rapidly evolving disaster,” the spokesperson said. “The result is tangible assistance reaching affected Nepalis now.

“The United States is continuing to assess the situation and will adjust its response as circumstances warrant.”

title: More than 1,200 dead in Nepal, China after flash floods - nhk.or.jp
description: More than 1,200 dead in Nepal, China after flash floods  nhk.or.jp
publisher.title: nhk.or.jp
full_article:
More than 1,200 people have died and over 4,700 others are unaccounted for in Nepal and China after massive flash floods and mudslides struck the border region of the two countries on August 26.

Nepali authorities say 1,204 people have been confirmed dead and the whereabouts of more than 4,200 people are unknown. Five Japanese nationals are among the missing.

China's state-run media report that 21 people were killed and more than 540 are missing on the Chinese side.

The combined death toll from both sides is 1,225.

Military personnel, police and others are engaged in search and rescue operations in Nepal. But as roads, power and communications remain disrupted over wide areas, rescuers are facing an uphill struggle.

Many people who have lost their homes remain evacuated. Authorities face the challenge of finding ways to deliver them relief supplies, and of maintaining hygiene in shelters to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.

Meanwhile, local media outlets say Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah told parliament on Wednesday that "the time has come for us to strongly present to the international community the disasters we are facing because of climate change."

Some experts say the flood was caused by a glacier that collapsed due to global warming.

Local media also reported that Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said that China, the US and India, as the top emitters of greenhouse gases, have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal. He indicated his country will seek compensation.

full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Tourists previously reported missing in Nepal have made contact with authorities, officials said Wednesday, as families of locals still unaccounted for after last week's catastrophic floods held symbolic funerals for their loved ones.

Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while another 590 from 39 countries remain missing following the Aug. 26 floods. At least 1,204 people have been killed and more than 4,200 are missing, according to the country's disaster management agency.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Wednesday that the number of Australians missing in the disaster had fallen from 43 to 38 after five were confirmed safe overnight.

“Amidst all of this tragedy, we are seeing some positive news. Today, another five Australians have been confirmed safe,” Albanese told reporters in Palau, where he is attending a regional summit.

“We hope, of course, for positive news further, and we’re doing everything we can to work with authorities,” Albanese added.

On Thursday, the Australian government said it would send a team of drone operators to Nepal within days to assist search and rescue efforts.

Sunil Sharma, a spokesperson for the Nepal Tourism Board, said at least five other tourists who were previously reported missing had contacted authorities by email or telephone in recent days.

It is thought the disaster happened when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream. The surge entered rivers flowing through Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges, carrying mud and rocks downstream.

Families hold symbolic funerals

Some families in Nuwakot, one of Nepal's worst-affected districts, have held symbolic funerals for relatives still missing, hoping to free their souls after they were presumed dead.

In Hindu tradition, cremation is an important final rite, and for some families, performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provides a sense of spiritual release.

Mukunda Rijal said his cousins and their daughters had not been found, prompting the family to perform a symbolic funeral for them.

Along the banks of the Trishuli River, a priest placed straw effigies representing the missing family members and covered them with small piles of wood before setting them alight. The symbolic funeral pyres were surrounded by offerings to Hindu deities as relatives gathered to perform the final rites.

Authorities in Nepal have also been burying recovered bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details to help match the remains with missing people and eventually return them to their families.

China builds access road for rescue crews

On the Chinese side, rescue crews completed a makeshift road to the disaster site at Gyirong Port on the Nepal border, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Wednesday.

Crews have been clearing access for heavy machinery to be used in the search at the border crossing complex, which was washed away by the floods. The road leading to the crossing was destroyed and buried under water, mud and rocks.

At least 21 people have been killed and 541 remain missing in China, according to the Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Survivors find shelter in Kathmandu

Some flood survivors are fleeing the devastation to seek shelter in Nepal's capital, Kathmandu.

Around 400 survivors, mostly from the town of Timure, about 110 kilometers (65 miles) west of Kathmandu, have been staying at the Yellow Gumba monastery. The shelter is being organized by locals and relatives, with relief supplies donated by individuals and charity organizations.

Riya Tamang, 21, who fled with her 10-month-old baby as the floodwaters approached, is among those taking shelter at the monastery. She lost her grandparents in the disaster.

“I was the last one to leave the house. It was so difficult to escape,” she said.

Her husband, who works as a cook in Gyirong town on the Chinese side of the border, also survived, and the couple now stays in touch through video calls.

Associated Press journalists Yasin Dar in Nuwakot, Nepal, Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.
